patient.name: Winston Clarke
patient.complaint: Three months of back pain, tiredness and recurrent chest infections
background: Jamaican heritage; retired postman in Brixton
Takes over-the-counter ibuprofen for back pain

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' in an older patient with back pain, anaemia, high calcium and renal impairment (CRAB), often with a high ESR.

points: Winston, 71, retired postman from Brixton, Jamaican heritage.
Three months of **lower back pain**, worse at night.
Exhausted; two chest infections since the summer.
Constipated, thirsty and 'a bit muddled', says his wife.

steps.lead: Winston is in his 70s and of **African-Caribbean** ethnicity, both risk factors. Ask about a known **MGUS**.

steps.title: GP bloods
steps.text: Normocytic anaemia, high calcium, renal impairment and a very high **ESR with near-normal CRP**.

visual.title: ESR
visual.label: Winston 98
visual.caption: ESR near 100 with a CRP of 6: paraprotein, not inflammation.

steps.lead: Winston has every letter of **CRAB**: calcium (thirst, constipation, confusion), renal, anaemia, bone pain. Plus **infections**.
**CRAB** features are what make myeloma 'myeloma-defining' rather than a precursor: Winston's end-organ damage means he needs treatment.

steps.q: Which single finding makes you most worried about myeloma in Winston?
o: High ESR with a normal CRP
steps.r: A **raised ESR with normal CRP** reflects excess paraprotein; myeloma anaemia is **normocytic**, not microcytic.

steps.lead: Winston's marrow holds a clone of **plasma cells** making a monoclonal **IgG** paraprotein, eroding bone and clogging his kidneys.
Winston's risks now: **pathological fracture**, **cord compression**, hypercalcaemic crisis, renal failure and **infection**.

steps.title: Myeloma vs bony metastases vs hyperparathyroidism
head: Feature
Myeloma
Bony metastases
Primary HPT

steps.lead: Winston has no migratory clots. **Trousseau's syndrome** belongs to **pancreatic** cancer, not myeloma: a classic mix-up.

investigation.exam: Expect best initial test (serum protein electrophoresis), confirmatory test (bone marrow biopsy), imaging (whole-body low-dose CT) and film findings (rouleaux).

steps.q: What is the best initial test for Winston?
steps.r: **SPEP** looks for the monoclonal band; marrow biopsy **confirms** after the screen.

steps.lead: Winston's full **myeloma screen**: SPEP, serum free light chains and urine **Bence Jones** protein, alongside FBC, calcium, renal function, ESR.

steps.title: Myeloma screen
steps.text: A monoclonal **IgG** band with a **suppressed PTH**: the calcium is not parathyroid.

steps.lead: Winston's blood film shows red cells stacked like coins: **rouleaux**, from paraprotein coating the cells.
Winston has **whole-body low-dose CT**: punched-out **lytic** lesions in his spine, pelvis and skull ('raindrop skull').

visual.title: Clonal plasma cells in marrow
visual.label: Winston 34%
visual.caption: More than **10% clonal plasma cells** confirms the diagnosis.

steps.lead: The **gold standard** is the myeloma screen plus **bone marrow biopsy**; Winston's shows 34% clonal plasma cells.

steps.text: A **bone scan** can look normal in myeloma: lesions are purely lytic, with little osteoblastic activity to take up tracer. Use CT.

steps.title: Investigating suspected myeloma
nodes: Myeloma screen: SPEP, free light chains, urine Bence Jones
Whole-body low-dose CT for lytic lesions
Bone marrow biopsy: >10% clonal plasma cells

management.exam: Expect emergencies (cord compression: emergency MRI), drugs to avoid (NSAIDs), bone protection (bisphosphonates) and transplant for fitter patients.

points: Week 2: Winston's back pain suddenly worsens.
Now his legs feel heavy and he is struggling to pass urine.
Bilateral leg weakness, sensory level at T10.

steps.q: What is the most urgent step?
steps.r: Back pain with **neurological deficit** in myeloma is **cord compression** until proven otherwise: MRI now, then urgent treatment.

steps.lead: Winston's cord compression needs **emergency MRI** and treatment. He must also avoid **NSAIDs**, which can tip his kidneys into failure.

steps.text: Do not give naproxen or ibuprofen for myeloma bone pain. **NSAIDs** can precipitate renal failure in an already damaged kidney.

steps.lead: Once stable, Winston starts a **bortezomib and dexamethasone**-based regimen. In older patients, the MPT protocol is an option.
At 71 with frailty, Winston is not a transplant candidate. A **younger, fitter** patient would go on to **autologous stem cell transplant**.
Winston takes a **bisphosphonate** for his bones, with supportive care for calcium, kidneys, pain and fractures.

visual.title: Winston's paraprotein on treatment
visual.caption: The paraprotein is the marker used to follow response.

steps.title: Managing myeloma
nodes: Emergencies first: cord compression, high calcium, AKI, sepsis
Fit and younger → autologous stem cell transplant
All: bisphosphonate, analgesia (no NSAIDs), infection care

science.exam: Expect mechanism questions: why lytic lesions and hypercalcaemia, why renal failure (cast nephropathy), why infections (immunoparesis).

steps.lead: Winston's disease is one **clone** of terminally differentiated B cells, all making the same IgG kappa paraprotein.
Myeloma cells release **RANKL and IL-6**, revving osteoclasts while suppressing osteoblasts: Winston's lytic lesions and high calcium.

steps.title: Why bones break in myeloma
steps.caption: No new bone forms, so ALP and bone scans are often normal.

steps.lead: Winston's free kappa chains filter into his tubules and form **casts**: 'myeloma kidney', worsened by his high calcium and dehydration.
Plasma cells crowd out Winston's marrow (**anaemia**) and he makes too little normal antibody (**immunoparesis**): hence the chest infections.

steps.q: Why does Winston keep getting chest infections despite a high total protein?
steps.r: The protein is **one useless monoclonal antibody**; normal immunoglobulins are suppressed (**immunoparesis**).

steps.lead: Winston may have had **MGUS** for years: a premalignant paraprotein that can progress to myeloma.

mcq.q: What does CRAB stand for in myeloma?
What is the median age at diagnosis of myeloma?
mcq.r: A disease of older adults; median **72**.

mcq.q: Which type of anaemia is typical of myeloma?
What is the best initial investigation for suspected myeloma?
What percentage of clonal plasma cells on marrow confirms myeloma?
Which blood film finding suggests myeloma?
mcq.r: Paraprotein makes red cells **stack like coins**.

mcq.q: What is the first-line imaging in suspected myeloma?
Which drug class should be avoided in myeloma?
What follows chemotherapy in younger, fitter patients?
Which cytokines drive osteoclast activity in myeloma?

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: which cell and what it makes.

points.p: Malignancy of plasma cells in bone marrow
Bone destruction, marrow failure, renal damage

prompts.q: Who gets myeloma? Give the risk factors.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: age and ethnicity in the stem.

prompts.q: What does CRAB stand for, with the symptoms of each?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: each letter has a symptom in the stem.

points.p: Renal impairment: raised urea and creatinine
Bone lesions: pain, lytic lesions, fractures

prompts.q: What are the complications of myeloma, and which cancer features must not be confused with it?

points.p: Renal failure, pathological fractures, hypercalcaemic crisis

points.why: Sepsis is a common cause of death.

points.p: Migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau's syndrome) is pancreatic cancer, not myeloma

prompts.q: What is the best initial test, what makes up the myeloma screen, and what is the typical blood pattern?

points.p: Serum free light chains and urine Bence Jones protein
Normocytic anaemia, high calcium, renal impairment

prompts.q: What confirms myeloma, and what do imaging and the blood film show?

points.p: Bone marrow biopsy: >10% clonal plasma cells

prompts.q: What is first-line and definitive treatment of myeloma?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: age and fitness decide.

prompts.q: How are myeloma emergencies and long-term complications managed, and what must be avoided?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: cord, calcium, kidney, sepsis.

points.p: Cord compression: emergency MRI and urgent treatment
Avoid NSAIDs: can precipitate renal failure
AKI and sepsis need urgent treatment

prompts.q: Why does myeloma cause bone lesions and hypercalcaemia?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: osteoclasts up, osteoblasts down.

points.p: Myeloma cells release RANKL and IL-6
Increased osteoclast and suppressed osteoblast activity
points.why: Why ALP and bone scans are often normal.

prompts.q: Why does myeloma cause renal impairment, anaemia and infections, and how does MGUS relate?

points.p: Light chain (Bence Jones) cast nephropathy, worse with calcium and dehydration
Marrow infiltration crowds out haematopoiesis: anaemia
MGUS is a premalignant precursor that can progress

glossary.multiple myeloma: Cancer of plasma cells in bone marrow producing a monoclonal antibody.
glossary.plasma cells: Fully mature B cells that make antibodies.
glossary.paraprotein: A single monoclonal immunoglobulin made in excess by one clone of cells.
glossary.M protein: Another name for the paraprotein band on electrophoresis.
glossary.IgG: The commonest immunoglobulin class and the commonest myeloma paraprotein.
glossary.CRAB: HyperCalcaemia, Renal impairment, Anaemia, Bone lesions: myeloma end-organ damage.
glossary.MGUS: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance: a small paraprotein without CRAB that can progress.
glossary.plasma cell dyscrasia: Any disorder of a clone of plasma cells making abnormal antibody.
glossary.SPEP: Serum protein electrophoresis; separates blood proteins to reveal a monoclonal band.
glossary.serum protein electrophoresis: Blood test separating proteins to show a monoclonal paraprotein band.
glossary.free light chains: Kappa or lambda antibody fragments measured in blood; the ratio becomes abnormal in myeloma.
glossary.Bence Jones protein: Free immunoglobulin light chains found in the urine in myeloma.
glossary.kappa: One of two types of antibody light chain.
glossary.lambda: One of two types of antibody light chain.
glossary.ESR: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate; very high in myeloma because paraprotein makes red cells clump.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein; an acute-phase marker that is often normal in myeloma.
glossary.normocytic: Red cells of normal size (normal MCV).
glossary.MCV: Mean cell volume, the average red cell size.
glossary.rouleaux: Red cells stacked like coins on a blood film, caused by excess protein.
glossary.lytic lesions: Areas where bone has been destroyed, seen as holes on imaging.
glossary.raindrop skull: Skull X-ray with many punched-out lytic holes in myeloma.
glossary.pathological fracture: A fracture through bone weakened by disease, after little or no trauma.
glossary.spinal cord compression: Pressure on the cord causing back pain, leg weakness, a sensory level and retention.
glossary.sensory level: A level on the trunk below which sensation is reduced; points to a cord lesion.
glossary.bone marrow biopsy: Sample of marrow, usually from the pelvis, to count plasma cells.
glossary.whole-body low-dose CT: CT of the whole skeleton at low radiation dose to find lytic lesions.
glossary.bortezomib: A proteasome inhibitor used to treat myeloma.
glossary.dexamethasone: A potent steroid used with other drugs to kill myeloma cells.
glossary.MPT: Melphalan, prednisolone and thalidomide; a regimen for older patients.
glossary.thalidomide: An immunomodulatory drug used in myeloma.
glossary.melphalan: An alkylating chemotherapy drug used in myeloma.
glossary.autologous stem cell transplant: High-dose chemotherapy then return of the patient's own stored stem cells.
glossary.bisphosphonates: Drugs that block osteoclasts and protect bone.
glossary.zoledronic acid: An IV bisphosphonate used for myeloma bone disease.
glossary.NSAIDs: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as naproxen and ibuprofen; harmful to kidneys in myeloma.
glossary.RANKL: Signal that activates osteoclasts to resorb bone.
glossary.IL-6: Interleukin-6; a cytokine that supports myeloma cell growth and bone resorption.
glossary.osteoclast: Bone cell that breaks bone down.
glossary.myeloma kidney: Kidney damage from light chain casts blocking the tubules.
glossary.cast nephropathy: Tubular blockage by protein casts made of light chains.
glossary.immunoparesis: Suppression of normal antibodies, causing infections.
glossary.Trousseau's syndrome: Migratory thrombophlebitis linked to pancreatic cancer, not myeloma.
glossary.Waldenström macroglobulinaemia: A lymphoma producing an IgM paraprotein.

technique.stem: A 74 year old man has 4 months of back pain and fatigue. He has had two chest infections this year. Investigations: haemoglobin 96 g/L (130–180), MCV 88 fL (80–100), adjusted calcium 2.84 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), creatinine 182 µmol/L (60–110), ESR 104 mm/h (<20), CRP 4 mg/L (<5).
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis from symptoms plus a bloods panel.
Bone pain, infections; normocytic anaemia, high calcium, renal impairment, ESR high but CRP normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: CRAB plus infections plus high ESR: **multiple myeloma**.

elim: Causes bone pain and high calcium, but not renal impairment, very high ESR and infections; ALP high.
High ESR but also high CRP, shoulder stiffness, normal calcium.
No anaemia or high ESR; PTH would be high.

steps.x: **B. Multiple myeloma.** Older patient + CRAB + high ESR, normal CRP = myeloma.

technique.stem: A 69 year old woman has back pain, anaemia and renal impairment. Serum protein electrophoresis shows an IgG paraprotein, and urine is positive for Bence Jones protein. Whole-body low-dose CT shows lytic lesions.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

steps.x: Confirmatory test after a positive screen.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Confirm with **bone marrow biopsy**: >10% clonal plasma cells.

elim: Already done; does not confirm marrow infiltration.

steps.x: **A. Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy.** SPEP screens; marrow confirms.

technique.stem: A 70 year old man was diagnosed with multiple myeloma last week. His back pain is poorly controlled and his GP started a new tablet 3 days ago. Creatinine has risen from 140 to 260 µmol/L (60–110).

steps.x: New analgesic followed by an acute rise in creatinine.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Not a cause of acute renal decline here.

technique.stem: A 66 year old man with multiple myeloma has worsening renal function. Urine is strongly positive for Bence Jones protein. Renal biopsy shows dense casts in the distal tubules.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his renal impairment?

steps.x: Free light chains in urine plus tubular casts.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Casts in tubules point to light chains, not immune complexes.

steps.x: **B. Light chain cast nephropathy.** Bence Jones + casts = cast nephropathy.

practice.stem: A 72 year old woman has 3 months of lower back pain, tiredness and constipation. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg and temperature 36.9°C. She has tenderness over L2. Investigations are shown.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Anaemia, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment and bone pain (CRAB) with a high ESR is myeloma. Hyperparathyroidism does not cause anaemia.

steps.x: Diagnosis from bone pain and bloods.

clues: lower back pain, tiredness and constipation
steps.x: Bone pain, constipation (calcium); anaemia, high calcium, renal impairment, high ESR.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Isolated raised ALP, normal calcium and renal function.
Shoulder and hip girdle stiffness; normal calcium.
No anaemia or renal impairment; PTH would be high.

steps.x: **A. Multiple myeloma.** CRAB in an older patient = myeloma.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man with suspected myeloma has a blood film examined. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg. ESR is 112 mm/h (<20).
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on the blood film?
practice.e: Paraprotein causes red cells to stack like coins (rouleaux) and raises the ESR.

steps.x: Paraprotein raises ESR and makes red cells stick.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Haemolysis, such as DIC or HUS.

practice.stem: A 76 year old man has diffuse bone pain. Serum protein electrophoresis shows an IgG paraprotein. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 140/84 mmHg. A lateral skull X-ray is taken.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on the skull X-ray?
practice.e: Myeloma causes multiple punched-out lytic lesions ('raindrop skull'). Pepper-pot skull is hyperparathyroidism; cotton wool is Paget's.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

steps.x: **C. Multiple punched-out lytic lesions.** Myeloma: lytic, not sclerotic.

practice.stem: A 68 year old man with known multiple myeloma has 2 days of worsening back pain and heavy legs. He has not passed urine for 10 hours. His pulse rate is 94 bpm, BP 136/82 mmHg and temperature 36.8°C. There is bilateral leg weakness with a sensory level at T10.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A sensory level with leg weakness and retention in myeloma is spinal cord compression from vertebral disease; it needs emergency MRI.

steps.x: Myeloma, back pain, leg weakness, retention, sensory level.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Saddle anaesthesia without a thoracic level; myeloma is the clue.
Ascending weakness with areflexia; no sensory level.
Confusion and dehydration, not a sensory level.
Would not give leg weakness or retention.

steps.x: **E. Spinal cord compression.** Back pain + neuro deficit in myeloma = cord compression.

practice.stem: A 73 year old woman is being investigated for back pain and renal impairment. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 130/78 mmHg. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal band. A 24 hour urine is sent.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on urine testing?
practice.e: Free immunoglobulin light chains spill into the urine as Bence Jones protein; they also damage tubules.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Free light chains in urine: **Bence Jones protein**.
**A. Bence Jones protein.** Myeloma urine: Bence Jones.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has fatigue and back pain. His pulse rate is 86 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. Haemoglobin is 100 g/L (130–180), calcium 2.74 mmol/L (2.20–2.60) and total protein 96 g/L (60–80).
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on serum protein electrophoresis?
practice.e: Myeloma produces a monoclonal paraprotein, usually IgG. A polyclonal rise suggests infection or liver disease.

steps.x: CRAB features with high total protein.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Waldenström macroglobulinaemia; IgG is commonest in myeloma.

steps.x: **A. Monoclonal IgG band.** Myeloma: monoclonal, usually IgG.

practice.stem: A 75 year old man has back pain, anaemia and a raised calcium. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg. Investigations are shown.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: Serum protein electrophoresis is the best initial test for myeloma; bone marrow biopsy confirms.

clues: back pain, anaemia and a raised calcium

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Prostate cancer; less likely here with ESR and renal picture.

steps.x: **E. Serum protein electrophoresis.** Suspect myeloma: SPEP first.

practice.stem: A 67 year old woman has an IgG paraprotein of 32 g/L and anaemia. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 126/74 mmHg. She is referred to haematology for imaging of the skeleton.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial imaging?
o: Plain X-ray of the lumbar spine
practice.e: Whole-body low-dose CT is first-line imaging for lytic lesions; bone scans miss them as there is little osteoblastic activity.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

steps.x: **E. Whole-body low-dose CT.** Myeloma imaging: whole-body low-dose CT.

practice.stem: A 69 year old woman with myeloma develops sudden back pain and leg weakness. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 140/84 mmHg. She has reduced sensation below the umbilicus.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
practice.e: Suspected spinal cord compression needs emergency MRI of the whole spine and urgent treatment.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Not urgent and misses lytic lesions.

steps.x: **C. Emergency MRI whole spine.** Cord compression: MRI now.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man has newly diagnosed multiple myeloma. He is fit, works full time and has no other conditions. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. He has completed induction chemotherapy.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next management?
practice.e: Younger, fitter patients have autologous stem cell transplant after induction chemotherapy.

steps.x: Next management for a fit, younger patient.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

steps.x: **B. Autologous stem cell transplantation.** Fit and younger: ASCT after induction.

practice.stem: A 72 year old woman has started bortezomib and dexamethasone for multiple myeloma with lytic lesions. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. Investigations are shown.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment to protect her bones?
practice.e: Bisphosphonates protect bone in myeloma. Calcium or vitamin D would worsen hypercalcaemia; NSAIDs harm the kidneys.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

steps.x: **E. Zoledronic acid.** Myeloma: bisphosphonates for all with bone disease.

practice.stem: A 71 year old man with myeloma has recurrent pneumonias. His total protein is high. His pulse rate is 98 bpm, BP 128/78 mmHg and temperature 38.1°C. Investigations are shown.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his recurrent infections?
practice.e: The clone makes one monoclonal antibody while normal immunoglobulins are suppressed (immunoparesis), causing infections.

steps.x: High total protein but low normal antibodies.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

steps.x: **C. Immunoparesis.** Lots of protein, all useless.
